traveler: Margarita / Marina / Pelagia, the Pearl of the Three Waters
title: Iconium to the Main: one woman seen through three waters
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The First Running: Thecla of Iconium

stops.name: Iconium, the window, and the voice of Paul
stops.campa: In Onesiphorus's house at Iconium the apostle Paul preaches continence and the resurrection to come, and a girl of the city, betrothed to the nobleman Thamyris, sits at the window across the street and does not move for three days and nights, neither to eat nor to rise, fastened to the sill by the word alone. Her mother Theocleia calls to her and she does not answer. This is Thecla, pearl not yet named pearl, and the voice she hears through the window is the first of the three waters this life will be baptized in.
suggested_refs: The Acts of Paul and Thecla (2nd c. apocryphon), the earliest surviving account
Byzantine icon of Thecla listening at the window
sources: Acts of Paul and Thecla (Acts of Paul, 2nd c.)

stops.name: Iconium, the stake in the theater, and the storm
stops.campa: Thamyris and Theocleia denounce her to the governor, who condemns her to burn rather than let a word from a stranger cost him a bride-price. In the theater the wood is stacked and lit; Thecla makes the sign of the cross over the pyre and steps in unafraid, as into a bridal chamber. God sends a cloud heavy with rain and hail; the fire hisses out under the downpour, and the crowd that came to watch her die watches instead a girl escape a fire that will not touch her, and slip ungrieved into the press toward the road Paul has taken.
suggested_refs: The theater of ancient Iconium, site of the extinguished pyre
sources: Acts of Paul and Thecla, 22 (2nd c.)

stops.name: Antioch, Alexander's assault in the street
stops.campa: Following Paul out of Iconium she comes to Antioch, and there a leading citizen named Alexander, struck by her beauty, seizes her in the open street meaning to have her. Thecla tears his cloak away and knocks the garland from his head, shaming a magistrate of Rome before the whole marketplace. Alexander drags her before the governor for the insult rather than confess the assault, and the city, delighted by the spectacle of a girl who fights back, condemns her to the wild beasts, to die for a violence she only refused.
suggested_refs: Ancient Antioch on the Orontes, first appearance of the city that will hold three of this life's timelines

stops.name: Antioch, the arena, the seals, and the self-baptism
stops.campa: In the amphitheater a lioness set to kill her instead lies at her feet and dies defending her from a bear and a lion. Queen Tryphaena, mourning her own dead daughter, has taken Thecla for her own and faints at the sight, staying the games for grief. Last, Thecla is thrown into a moat of man-eating seals: she flings herself in first, crying that she baptizes herself in the name of Jesus Christ on this, her last day. Lightning splits the water, and the seals float up dead all around her, unharmed.
stops.quote: In the name of Jesus Christ do I baptize myself on the last day.
stops.quote_source: Acts of Paul and Thecla, 34 (2nd c. apocryphon)
suggested_refs: The seal-pool self-baptism, a recurring image in early Christian sarcophagus carving

stops.name: Iconium, the return, and the mother who will not open the door
stops.campa: Freed by the governor at Tryphaena's plea, Thecla cuts her hair, puts on a man's tunic, and finds Paul again to be sent out to teach in his name. She returns once more to Iconium hoping to bring her mother Theocleia to the faith that has cost her a stake and an arena; her mother will not receive her. Thecla leaves the house of her childhood a last time, wearing a man's clothes, carrying no dowry but two deaths refused, and turns south toward the mountain city of Seleucia.
suggested_refs: The house of Theocleia at Iconium, the closed door of the tradition

stops.name: Seleucia, the cave, the long teaching, and the earth that opens
stops.campa: For decades Thecla lives in a cave above Seleucia, teaching, healing the sick who climb to her, and converting the daughters of the pagan city, until physicians jealous of a healer who takes no fee send men to violate her old age. She prays, and the rock face of the mountain opens and receives her living body into itself, leaving her enemies clutching a torn piece of her veil. The tradition keeps her not as a grave but as a door in stone: the first runaway of this book to become, instead of a body, a threshold.
suggested_refs: The cave-shrine of Hagia Thekla (Meryemlik) above Silifke, ancient Seleucia
sources: Life and Miracles of Saint Thecla (5th c.)

stops.name: Antioch, birth, and the death of the mother
stops.campa: Margaret is born in Antioch on the Orontes in the year 291, daughter of the pagan priest the canon calls Theodosius and, in another hand, Aedesius: the record keeps both names honestly, as it keeps her under two others still to come. Her mother dies soon after the birth, and the infant is given to a nurse to raise outside the city, a woman who is, unknown to the priest, a Christian in secret. The girl who will be called pearl begins her life carried already between a father's temple and a nurse's hidden altar.
suggested_refs: Golden Legend manuscript illumination of Margaret's birth at Antioch
sources: Golden Legend (Jacobus de Voragine, 1275), Life of St. Margaret

stops.name: Antioch, the nurse's sheep, and the conversion of a child
stops.campa: Raised outside Antioch's walls, Margaret tends her nurse's sheep on the hillside and is taught the faith her father would kill her for, and takes to it entire, as a child takes to a story that turns out to be true. When Theodosius learns his daughter has been baptized in secret he disowns her outright. She keeps the sheep and keeps the faith both, unhoused by her father's roof but sheltered, she says later, by a greater one: the first exile of every timeline this one life will carry.
suggested_refs: Iconography of Saint Margaret with a shepherd's crook alongside the dragon
sources: Golden Legend, Life of St. Margaret

stops.name: Antioch, Olybrius, the refusal, the rods
stops.campa: At fifteen, keeping the flock by the road, Margaret is seen by Olybrius, the Roman diocese of the East, who wants her for wife or concubine and sends for her. She tells him plainly she is a Christian and will have no husband but Christ. He has her beaten bloody with rods in the public street and thrown into a cell to break her overnight, certain a shepherd girl's faith will not survive till morning. It is the oldest bargain offered to every runaway bride in this family: recant and marry, or keep the name and be broken.
stops.quote: O what shame is it to you, when you read the pain of Christ and the glory, and believe one thing and deny another.
stops.quote_source: Golden Legend (Caxton translation, 1483), Life of Saint Margaret
suggested_refs: The trial-square of Olybrius in Antioch, as painted in countless Margaret altarpieces
sources: Golden Legend, Life of St. Margaret

stops.name: Antioch, the cell, the dragon, the cross that opens it
stops.campa: In the dark of the cell Margaret prays God to show her the enemy she fights in the flesh, that faith not remain a thing only spoken. Satan answers by becoming a serpent-dragon of enormous size, opens its jaws, and swallows her whole. Inside the belly of the beast she does not despair; she makes the sign of the cross with her bound hands, and the cross, growing in the dark gullet, bursts the dragon open and sets her free unmarked. A second devil appears in another shape at once; she throws him down and sets her foot on his neck.
stops.quote: Lie still, thou fiend, under the feet of a woman.
stops.quote_source: Golden Legend (Caxton, 1483), Life of Saint Margaret
suggested_refs: Raphael's Saint Margaret (Louvre), Titian's Saint Margaret, the dragon-slayer iconography of Western art
sources: Golden Legend, Life of St. Margaret

stops.name: Antioch, the public square, fire and iron, the rope
stops.campa: Brought again before Olybrius and the crowd, Margaret refuses the gods of Rome a second time, in daylight, before witnesses who cannot later claim they were not there. The authorities burn her with torches, tear her sides with iron combs, and bind her with rope to drag her through the square: a public unmaking meant to be watched to its end, so no one converted by rumor could later doubt it happened. She endures it singing, the Legend says, and the crowd that came to see a girl broken begins instead to weep.
stops.quote: Christ gave Himself over to the death for me, and I desire gladly to die for Christ.
stops.quote_source: Golden Legend (Caxton, 1483), Life of Saint Margaret
suggested_refs: The iron combs and torches of Margaret's iconography, alongside the cross and crown
sources: Golden Legend, Life of St. Margaret

stops.name: Antioch, the sealed vessel, the coronal event, the beheading
stops.campa: Last, they seal Margaret into a great vessel of water to drown her where fire and iron have failed. At the moment of her sealing the sky over Antioch opens with thunder, and a plasma crown descends and forms itself around her head, visible over the whole square; thousands of the watching crowd convert on the spot, undone by the light more than by the argument. Olybrius, seeing his own authority burn away with every witness, orders her beheading before the conversions can spread further, and it is done outside the walls that same hour.
stops.quote: Father Almighty, I yield to you thankings that You have suffered me to come to this glory, beseeching You to pardon them that pursue me... if any woman with child travailing in any place, call on me, that thou wilt keep her from peril, and that the child may be delivered from her belly without any hurt of his members.
stops.quote_source: Golden Legend (Caxton, 1483), Life of Saint Margaret
suggested_refs: The coronal event: sky, thunder, and crown of light, Margaret's most singular miracle
her patronage of women in childbirth, drawn directly from this final prayer
sources: Golden Legend, Life of St. Margaret

segments.name: The Eastern Mirror: Marina the Great Martyr

stops.name: Antioch, the cell, the small demon, and the hammer (the eastern glass)
stops.campa: Seen through Byzantine eyes the same cell holds a different enemy: not a great serpent but a small black demon that creeps to Marina, for so the East calls her, of-the-sea, in the dark to frighten her from her faith. She finds a copper hammer forgotten in the corner of the dungeon, seizes the demon by the horns, sets her foot on his neck, and beats him until he begs. Where the West paints a dragon and a hand-cross, the East paints a hammer and a devil small enough for one woman's sandal: the same cell, the same night, another set of eyes.
stops.quote: Depart from me, O lawless one.
stops.quote_source: Greek Synaxarion, Vita of the Great Martyr Marina (17 July)
suggested_refs: Byzantine icons of St. Marina holding a demon by the hair with a hammer raised
sources: Orthodox Church in America, Lives of the Saints (17 July)

stops.name: Antioch, the vat of water, and the dove (the eastern glass)
stops.campa: Where the western record has iron combs and a dragging rope, the eastern vita has Marina bound and lowered into a great vat of water to drown her before the crowd: the same threatened drowning her sister-timeline Margaret suffers by a sealed vessel. A white dove descends from the opened air, and with it a great light; her bonds fall away of themselves, and she rises from the vat healed of every wound, not a scar left on her, to the astonishment of the guards who had tied the knots that same morning.
suggested_refs: The dove-and-vat miracle unique to Marina's eastern vita
sources: Greek Synaxarion, Vita of the Great Martyr Marina

stops.name: Antioch, the beheading (the eastern glass)
stops.campa: The eastern day ends where the western day ends, at the same hour, on the same ground: the governor, seeing his authority dissolve with every convert who has watched a girl walk unmarked out of fire, water, and a dragon's belly, orders her head struck off outside the city. The Greek calendar keeps her on the seventeenth of July as Great Martyr and Vanquisher of Demons, hammer in hand in her icons where the West gives her a cross: two glasses turned on one flame, the coronal light of one stop reappearing here as a nimbus over Marina's head.
suggested_refs: Feast of Great Martyr Marina (Margaret) of Antioch, 17 July, Orthodox calendar
sources: Orthodox Church in America, Lives of the Saints (17 July)

stops.name: Antioch, the soldiers at the door
stops.campa: In the early fourth century, in a Christian household of Antioch, a girl of fifteen named Pelagia is at home when soldiers come pounding at the door, sent, though the brief record does not say by whom, only that persecution is loose in the city again, to take her, virgin and unmarried, for whatever use soldiers in such an hour intend. She hears them on the stair. Ambrose of Milan and John Chrysostom will later preach her as a model of chastity defended by any means necessary, including the last one; the household has only the length of the staircase to decide.
suggested_refs: Ambrose of Milan, De Virginibus, holding Pelagia before his consecrated virgins
sources: Ambrose of Milan, De Virginibus III

stops.name: Antioch, the leap from the housetop
stops.campa: Rather than be taken, Pelagia asks leave to change her dress, climbs to the top of the house, and without hesitating throws herself from the roof to the street below. She dies of the fall, fifteen years old, choosing the one door still hers to open. The record is almost too brief to be a story: a girl, a rooftop, a decision made faster than the soldiers can climb the stairs, and it is exactly that brevity the church keeps and reveres: no debate, no argument, only a body given entire rather than divided.
stops.quote: When a group of soldiers came to arrest her, this girl of fifteen threw herself from the top of the house, and died.
stops.quote_source: Henschel, dictionary 'Los Santos' (cited in the essay tradition); cf. Ambrose, De Virginibus III
suggested_refs: The leap from the housetop, invoked directly at Joan's trial as Article 65

stops.name: Antioch, the homilies of Ambrose and Chrysostom
stops.campa: Decades on, two of the greatest voices of the fourth-century church take up Pelagia's leap as doctrine. In Milan, Ambrose holds her before his consecrated virgins as proof that chastity may be defended by any means, even a death chosen outright. In Antioch itself, John Chrysostom, still a priest of his own city, preaches her memory to the same streets she fell through, praising the girl who out-argued her executioners by never letting them speak to her at all. Two bishops, two cities, one falling body: the church's first attempt to make doctrine of a leap it will not explain away.
suggested_refs: Ambrose, De Virginibus III; John Chrysostom's Antiochene homilies on virgin martyrs
sources: John Chrysostom, homilies on Pelagia of Antioch

segments.name: The Pearl of Antioch: Pelagia the Penitent

stops.name: Antioch, the courtesan called Margaret
stops.campa: A woman older than the dragon-life and later than the leap moves through the same city under a third water: an actress and courtesan of Antioch, foremost and noblest of its women, dressed in nothing the Golden Legend can name without listing gold, silver, and precious stones. She goes by Margaret: for the pomp of my clothing, she will say of herself, though it is not the name of her baptism, which no one in the city yet knows. Vain and variable of courage, not chaste of body, she is, the chronicle insists, still herself entire, waiting for a reason to change.
stops.quote: For the pomp of my clothing men call me Margaret.
stops.quote_source: Golden Legend, Life of St. Pelagia; cf. essays/215_runaway_bride.md
suggested_refs: Golden Legend description of Pelagia/Margaret as 'foremost and noblest of the women of Antioch'
sources: Golden Legend, Life of St. Pelagia

stops.name: Antioch, the synod, and Nonnus of Heliopolis
stops.campa: A council of bishops gathers in Antioch, among them Nonnus, bishop of Heliopolis: Barbara's own city, whose stone tower stands two hundred kilometers south of this street, its arc touching Margaret's without either woman knowing it. Margaret passes the assembled fathers in procession, borne on a litter, scented, jeweled, laughing with her companions, careless of the churchmen's stares. Nonnus alone cannot look away; delighted and troubled at once by her hair and the shape of her body through the silk, he weeps before his brothers that he has not brought God so rich an offering in a single day's prayer as this woman brings her own vanity.
stops.quote: The adornments and array of one common woman hath surmounted in one day all the wisdom of all my life.
stops.quote_source: Golden Legend (Caxton, 1483), Life of St. Pelagienne
suggested_refs: Nonnus, Bishop of Heliopolis, cross-reference saint_barbara.journey.json, same city
sources: Golden Legend, Life of St. Pelagia

stops.name: Antioch, she seeks Nonnus, and throws herself into mercy
stops.campa: Struck by what she overhears of Nonnus's grief, Margaret comes herself to the church door and sends in asking for him. He will not receive her alone, keeping the other fathers present as witnesses against his own reported weakness, and she is made to wait outside the very walls that keep other women in. When admitted at last, she falls at his feet before the assembled clergy, weeping, and begs the baptism that will unmake the name Margaret and give her back the name her parents chose before either of her lives began: Pelagia, of the open sea.
suggested_refs: The Golden Legend's account of Margaret's plea at the church door
sources: Golden Legend, Life of St. Pelagia

stops.name: Antioch, the baptism under the birth name
stops.campa: Nonnus baptizes her himself, before the bishops of the synod, under the name Pelagia: not Margaret, the pomp-name, but the water-name, of-the-open-sea, the third of this life's names to carry that same tide. She gives every jewel, every garment of gold and silver, to the poor of Antioch through Nonnus's hand, keeping nothing back, the pearl divesting itself of every pearl it ever wore. The city that knew her as the richest of its women watches her walk out of the church in plain wool, and does not yet know whether to call it scandal or miracle.
suggested_refs: The baptismal font tradition associated with Pelagia's conversion at Antioch
sources: Golden Legend, Life of St. Pelagia
James the Deacon, Vita Sanctae Pelagiae (5th c.)

stops.name: Antioch, the devil at the door, driven off
stops.campa: In the small room Nonnus has found her, the devil comes to Pelagia in the night in her old shape, reminding her of the silks and the litter and the men who paid to watch her walk. She answers him with the sign of the cross alone, no argument, no bargaining: the same gesture that once burst a dragon and once felled a demon under a sandaled foot, deployed now against a subtler enemy than either. He flees the room as the dragon fled the cross inside Margaret's body, and Pelagia is left alone with the wool dress and the decision still ahead of her.
suggested_refs: The devil-driven-off-by-the-cross motif, recurring across all three virgin martyrs of this triad
sources: Golden Legend, Life of St. Pelagia

stops.name: Antioch, the garment of Nonnus, and the flight to Jerusalem
stops.campa: Before dawn Pelagia takes one of Nonnus's own garments, a monk's habit, man's clothing, the cut hair implied though the Legend does not linger on it, and slips out of Antioch alone, leaving no household, no dowry, no farewell to the companions who knew her rich. She turns south and east toward Jerusalem, toward the Mount of Olives, three hundred kilometers of road walked as a man walks it, under a name now doubly hers: Pelagia to the church that baptized her, and soon Pelagius to the brothers who will never learn otherwise while she lives.
suggested_refs: The road from Antioch to Jerusalem, walked in a bishop's borrowed garment
sources: Golden Legend, Life of St. Pelagia

stops.name: The Mount of Olives, the cell, brother Pelagius
stops.campa: On the Mount of Olives, within sight of the garden where Christ kept his own vigil, Pelagia builds herself a narrow cell and takes up the life of a solitary monk under the name Pelagius, known to the brothers of the mountain only as a beardless eunuch of unusual holiness, fasting hard, speaking little, admitting no one. Pilgrims climb to be blessed by the famous eunuch monk of Olivet without guessing what the Legend already knows: that the pearl of Antioch and the anchorite of the Mount are the same flesh, the same water, differently dressed.
suggested_refs: The Mount of Olives hermit cells above Gethsemane and the Church of the Ascension, adjacent to jesus.journey.json and mary_magdalene.journey.json Jerusalem pins
sources: Golden Legend, Life of St. Pelagia
James the Deacon, Vita Sanctae Pelagiae (5th c. eyewitness account)

stops.name: The Mount of Olives, the death of brother Pelagius, and the truth
stops.campa: Years into the solitary life, brother Pelagius dies in the cell on Olivet, and the brothers who come to wash the body for burial find not the eunuch monk they have known for a decade but a woman, wasted by fasting to nothing, no trace left of the silks or the litter of Antioch. Word runs back down the mountain to Jerusalem and further, to the city she fled, where those who remember the actress called Margaret learn only now, at the graveside, which of her names was true. The church fixes her memory on the eighth of October, the date this cell finally tells its secret.
suggested_refs: Feast of St. Pelagia the Penitent, 8 October
sources: James the Deacon, Vita Sanctae Pelagiae (5th c.)
Golden Legend, Life of St. Pelagia

segments.name: The Runaway Bride: Margaret-Pelagia and Marina the Monk

stops.name: Antioch, the wedding night, the midnight flight
stops.campa: In the version the Golden Legend keeps folded inside its own chapter on Pelagia, a bride called by two names, Margaret and Pelagia both, the record insisting on the doubling rather than resolving it, is married in the customary way and lies down in her husband's house. That night she does not go to him. At midnight she rises, commits herself to God alone, cuts off her hair with her own hand, and dresses herself in a man's habit taken from she does not say where, and is gone before her husband wakes to find the bed half-empty and the door unbarred.
stops.quote: Margaret had twin names; she was called Margaret and Pelagia... and that night she kept from the company of her husband. At midnight, she committed herself to God, cut off her hair, and clad herself in the habit of a man.
stops.quote_source: Golden Legend, Life of St. Pelagia (as carried in essays/215_runaway_bride.md)
suggested_refs: The twin-named Margaret-Pelagia of the Golden Legend, invoked 128 times at Joan's trial
sources: Golden Legend, Life of St. Pelagia

stops.name: Antioch, the monastery gate, 'brother Pelagia'
stops.campa: She flees not to the desert alone but to a monastery of monks, and asks entrance in her cut hair and borrowed habit; the brothers, deceived exactly as she means them to be, take her in and call her brother Pelagia: the masculine title laid directly over the feminine name, a contradiction the Legend records without comment, as though it were the whole point. She lives out her life among them undiscovered, one more runaway bride keeping the same trick that saved Thecla and will save Marina after her: the habit changes what men see; the name, half-changed, is where the truth still hides.
stops.quote: Then she fled to a monastery of monks, who called her brother Pelagia.
stops.quote_source: Golden Legend, Life of St. Pelagia (as carried in essays/215_runaway_bride.md)
suggested_refs: The 'brother Pelagia' formula, the exact hinge-phrase of the essay 215_runaway_bride.md
sources: Golden Legend, Life of St. Pelagia

stops.name: Al-Qalamoun, near Tripoli: a father resolves to raise his daughter as a monk
stops.campa: Two hundred years later and eastward down the same coast, in a village near Tripoli in Lebanon, a Christian merchant named Eugenius loses his wife and is left with an infant daughter, Marina. Nearing old age he resolves to give away his goods and enter the monastery of Qannoubine in the mountains above, and grieves that he must first place the child in a convent of women, apart from him. Marina, still young, will not hear of the separation: let her go with him as a boy, she says, and be raised a monk at his side rather than a stranger in a house of strangers.
suggested_refs: Al-Qalamoun on the Lebanese coast south of Tripoli, Marina the Monk's home village
sources: Vita of Marina the Monk (Syriac/Greek, medieval)

stops.name: Qannoubine, the Kadisha Valley, the monk Marinos
stops.campa: Eugenius shaves his daughter's head, dresses her as a boy, and brings her to Qannoubine in the cliffside valley the Syriac tongue calls Kadisha, the holy valley, where they take their vows together and share a cell as father and son. She is known now as the monk Marinos, and grows into the discipline so entirely, in the fasts, the silence, the labor of hauling the monastery's grain to and from the town below by mule, that no brother in twenty years suspects the body under the habit is a woman's, not even the abbot who will one day condemn her unheard.
suggested_refs: The Qannoubine Monastery in the Kadisha Valley, UNESCO World Heritage Site

stops.name: Qannoubine, the false accusation, the child raised at the gate
stops.campa: Sent down with the mule to fetch supplies, Marinos lodges at an inn whose keeper's daughter is got with child by a soldier; to save herself she names the young monk as the father. The innkeeper storms to the monastery; Marinos, given the choice between confessing falsely or exposing her own sex to clear her name, kneels and confesses to a sin she has not committed, choosing shame as a man over the truth as a woman. She is driven from the gate, and when the child is born it is given to her, the disgraced monk, to raise alone outside the walls for ten years on borrowed milk.
suggested_refs: The false-paternity ordeal shared across the medieval 'transvestite saint' cycle

stops.name: Qannoubine, the death of Marinos, and the truth at the grave
stops.campa: Marinos dies still uncleared, still confessed to a sin never hers, and the brothers who come to wash the body for burial find, as on the Mount of Olives, a woman where they expected a man: the same discovery, the same grief for having doubted, a mountain valley answering a mountain garden a world away. The abbot and monks fall on their knees before the body begging forgiveness of the saint they condemned unheard, and the innkeeper who accused her repents at the news. The child she raised on borrowed milk becomes a monk of the same house, keeping in silence the second half of a lie that was never hers to begin with.
suggested_refs: The vindication-at-death scene, mirrored by brother Pelagius's revelation on the Mount of Olives

segments.name: The Voice: Domrémy, Rouen, and the Plaque on the Main

stops.name: Domrémy, her father's garden
stops.campa: In the garden behind Jacques d'Arc's house at Domrémy a summer voice comes to a girl of thirteen, and behind the first voice, Michael's, come two more, crowned in rich and precious crowns: Catherine, and Margaret, riding every wave of every name this life has carried since Antioch. It is the same voice that once prayed inside a dragon's belly, that leapt from a housetop at fifteen, that fled a wedding bed at midnight, that raised another woman's child in silence for ten years without complaint, arriving now in Lorraine to counsel a shepherd girl who will, within five years, be asked to make exactly the same kind of leap.
suggested_refs: The birthplace house of Jacques d'Arc at Domrémy (shared pin, see joan_of_arc.journey.json)

stops.name: Lyon, Gerson's De Mirabili Victoria
stops.campa: In his cell at the Celestine convent in Lyon, old and in exile, the theologian Jean Gerson finishes a short defense of the Maid a month after Orléans is relieved: De Mirabili Victoria, on the miraculous victory, citing the precedent of Thecla, Pelagia, and Marina as church mothers who dressed as men, faced the devil directly, and answered to no authority but God's own voice. He will be dead within two months. It is the first time in this book the timelines are named together in a single sentence by someone outside the family of their own legend, in defense of a fourth woman entirely.
suggested_refs: Jean Gerson, De Mirabili Victoria, 14 May 1429, citing Thecla, Pelagia, and Marina by name
sources: Jean Gerson, De Mirabili Victoria (14 May 1429)

stops.name: Embrun, Gelu's dissertation on the Maid
stops.campa: In the mountain seat of Embrun, Archbishop Jacques Gelu writes his own dissertation on the Maid of Orléans, De Puella Aurelianensi, reaching for the same three names Gerson reached for in Lyon: Thecla, Pelagia, Marina, to argue that a woman's authority, when it comes directly from God, need not apologize for the clothes it wears to do God's work. Two churchmen in two cities, writing within weeks of each other without conferring, arrive at the same short list of precedents, as if the runaway brides of the fourth and fifth centuries had been waiting fourteen hundred years for a case exactly like this one.
suggested_refs: Jacques Gelu, De Puella Aurelianensi Dissertatio, 1429, the second of the twin defenses
sources: Jacques Gelu, De Puella Aurelianensi Dissertatio (1429)

stops.name: Beaurevoir, the leap relived
stops.campa: At Beaurevoir, against Catherine's daily counsel but not, the trial will insist later, against Margaret's own oldest example, Jehanne climbs to the tower window and leaps sixty feet to the ground rather than be handed to the English and see Compiègne burned. She is found unbroken, senseless, unbleeding: Pelagia's fifteen-year-old leap from an Antioch housetop relived eleven centuries later by a girl who has never read the Golden Legend but carries its logic anyway: some doors are better gone through at a fall than opened. Article 65 of the accusation will call it despair. This family has another word for it.
stops.quote: I did it not out of despair, but in the hope of saving my body and of going to succour the good people in need.
stops.quote_source: Trial of condemnation, session of 14 March 1431 (shared pin, see joan_of_arc.journey.json)

stops.name: Rouen, Margaret invoked one hundred and twenty-eight times
stops.campa: Across the record of Rouen's trial, the name Margaret is invoked one hundred and twenty-eight times, more than any other word save God and the king, as Jehanne answers question after question about the voice that speaks the tongue of France, beautiful, sweet and low, and will not, asked directly, speak English, for she is not on the English side. The judges who count every heresy do not count how often they themselves say the name trying to trap her with it. Margaret, examined by proxy through her servant's mouth for eighty-nine days, never once appears in the court to answer for herself.

stops.name: Obernburg am Main, the Anna-Kapelle, and the three holy maids
stops.campa: On the Nothelferaltar of the little Anna-Kapelle at Obernburg am Main, some fifty kilometers up the river from Frankfurt, a carved verse fixes the three virgin martyrs together for good, past every timeline, past every twin name: Margaretha mit dem Wurm, Barbara mit dem Turm, Katharina mit dem Radl: Margaret with the dragon, Barbara with the tower, Catherine with the wheel, das sind die drei heiligen Madl, those are the three holy maids. The chapel keeps no record of Thecla, Pelagia, or Marina by name, only the dragon-image that carries all their weight at once: the last water this life is seen through, a plaque instead of a voice.
stops.quote: Margaretha mit dem Wurm, Barbara mit dem Turm, Katharina mit dem Radl, das sind die drei heiligen Madl.
stops.quote_source: Nothelferaltar inscription, Annakapelle, Obernburg am Main (late 18th c.); essays/213_las_tres_virgenes_martires.md
